parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
An ideal gas is assumed to consist of atoms or molecules that behave as hard, identical spheres that are in continuous motion and undergo elastic collisions.

State two further assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.

markscheme_points.text: e.g. time of collisions negligible compared to time between collisions; no intermolecular forces (except during collisions); random motion (of molecules); large numbers of molecules; (total) volume of molecules negligible compared to volume of containing vessel or average/mean separation large compared with size of molecules; any two

hints: Hint 1: Think about what an ideal gas ignores in real life. Do widely spaced tiny atoms pull on each other for most of the time, and how much space do they actually take up compared to the whole box?

Hint 2: Recall the other standard idealisations - motion is completely disordered with huge numbers of particles, and collisions themselves take up almost no time compared to the free flight between them.
parts.proper_answer: Any two: no intermolecular forces except during collisions; volume of molecules negligible compared to volume of vessel; molecules move randomly; large number of molecules; duration of collision negligible compared to time between collisions.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the idealised gas**
Imagine a huge crowd of tiny hard balls flying around a large room. For the simple kinetic theory to work, life has to be kept very simple. You are already told they move continuously and bounce elastically, so think what else must be ignored.

Step 2: **Forces and size**
A real gas has weak attractions and the atoms themselves have size. In the ideal model we say there are no intermolecular forces at all except during the instant of collision, and the total volume of all the molecules is negligible compared to the volume of the container. That is the same as saying the average separation is much larger than the molecular diameter.

Step 3: **Motion and statistics**
Other acceptable assumptions are that motion is random in direction, that there are very large numbers of molecules so averages are meaningful, and that the time of a collision is negligible compared to the time between collisions.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: Helium-4 ($^{4}_{2}\text{He}$) may be assumed to be an ideal gas.
parts.text: Show that the mass of one atom of helium-4 is $6.6 \times 10^{-24}\text{ g}$.
hints: Hint 1: The name helium-4 tells you the mass of one mole. Think about how many atoms are in one mole and how you would share that molar mass equally among them.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link mole to one atom**
Helium-4 has nucleon number 4, so one mole of helium-4 atoms has mass $4.0 \text{ g}$. One mole contains the Avogadro number of atoms, $$N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$$ So the mass of one atom is the molar mass divided by the number of atoms in a mole.

Step 2: **Calculate**
$$m = \frac{4.0 \text{ g}}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} \approx 6.64 \times 10^{-24} \text{ g} \approx 6.6 \times 10^{-24} \text{ g}$$ This shows the required result.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The mean kinetic energy $E_{\text{K}}$ of an atom of an ideal gas is given by the expression
$$E_{\text{K}} = \frac{3}{2}kT.$$
Calculate the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) speed of a helium-4 atom at a temperature of $27^{\circ}\text{C}$.
hints: Hint 1: You are given two different ways to write the same mean kinetic energy. Think about what $E_K$ equals in terms of temperature, and what it also equals in terms of mass and mean-square speed.
parts.proper_answer: $T = 300 \text{ K}$, $m = 6.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$, $\frac{1}{2}m\langle c^2 \rangle = \frac{3}{2}kT$ gives r.m.s. speed $= \sqrt{\langle c^2 \rangle} \approx 1.4 \times 10^3 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Equate the two forms of mean energy**
Temperature is a measure of average random translational kinetic energy. For one atom, $$E_K = \frac{3}{2}kT$$ and also from mechanics, $$E_K = \frac{1}{2}m\langle c^2 \rangle$$ where $\langle c^2 \rangle$ is the mean-square speed. So: $$\frac{1}{2}m\langle c^2 \rangle = \frac{3}{2}kT$$

Step 2: **Convert to SI units**
$27^{\circ}\text{C}$ must become kelvin: $$T = 27 + 273 = 300 \text{ K}$$ The mass from (b)(i) is in grams, convert to kilograms: $$m = 6.6 \times 10^{-24} \text{ g} = 6.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$$ Boltzmann constant $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J K}^{-1}$.

Step 3: **Solve for mean-square speed then r.m.s. speed**
$$\langle c^2 \rangle = \frac{3kT}{m} = \frac{3 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300}{6.6 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 1.88 \times 10^6 \text{ m}^2 \text{ s}^{-2}$$ The r.m.s. speed $c_{rms} = \sqrt{\langle c^2 \rangle}$: $$c_{rms} = \sqrt{1.88 \times 10^6} \approx 1.4 \times 10^3 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This very large speed is typical for light helium atoms at room temperature.
